common.sentence: Em Braga, Eva diz: «O guia encontrou-nos, a mim e ao Rui, na estação.»

language_specific.grammar: Target: postverbal first-person plural object pronoun refers to the speaker Eva and Rui; it is joined to the affirmative finite verb by a hyphen.
language_specific.usage: Target: This enclitic placement is standard in Portugal.

common.sentence: Em Faro, Eva diz: «O Rui chegou; nunca lhe telefonei.»

language_specific.grammar: Target: Nunca places the indirect object pronoun before the finite verb; it refers to Rui.
language_specific.usage: Target: This triggered proclisis is standard in Portugal.

common.sentence: Em Faro, Eva diz: «Pedi as chaves ao Rui; ele entregou-mas ontem.»

language_specific.grammar: Target: Mas combines me with as, referring to the speaker and the keys, after the finite verb.
language_specific.usage: Target: This combined enclitic form is used in Portugal.

common.sentence: Em Braga, Eva diz ao Rui: «Tenho o mapa; mostro-to depois.»

language_specific.grammar: Target: to combines te, referring to Rui, with o, referring to mapa; it follows first-person singular present indicative mostro.
language_specific.usage: Target: This combined enclitic form is used in Portugal.

common.sentence: Em Lisboa, Ana diz: «Guardei a mochila no cacifo do ginásio.»

language_specific.usage: Target: Cacifo is a personal storage locker in Portugal; armário or guarda-volumes is common in Brazil.

common.sentence: No Porto, Rui diz: «O mercado fecha cedo.»

language_specific.pronunciation: Target: In Portugal, the unstressed e before r in mercado can be realized as [ɨ].
language_specific.usage: Target: Recognize this ordinary spelling alongside a reduced Portuguese pronunciation.

common.sentence: Em Faro, Sara diz: «Comprei estes bolos na pastelaria da esquina.»

language_specific.usage: Target: In Portugal, a pastelaria sells cakes and pastries; confeitaria is a common Brazilian term.

common.sentence: Em Braga, Rita diz: «O concerto de ontem foi fixe!»

language_specific.usage: Target: Fixe is an informal positive adjective in Portugal; legal is common in Brazil.

common.sentence: Em Faro, Ana diz: «Esse desenho no cartão é giro.»

language_specific.grammar: Target: Masculine singular adjective agrees with desenho.
language_specific.usage: Target: Giro is an informal positive adjective in Portugal; bonito is common in Brazil.

common.sentence: Em Lisboa, Rui diz: «A minha tia trouxe fotografias da família.»

language_specific.pronunciation: Target: In careful Lisbon speech, t before [i] is plain [t]; in São Paulo it is commonly [tʃ].
language_specific.usage: Target: Recognize this pronunciation in Portugal speech.

common.sentence: Em Lisboa, Eva diz: «O dia começa às seis para mim.»

language_specific.pronunciation: Target: In careful Lisbon speech, d before [i] is plain [d]; in São Paulo it is commonly [dʒ].
language_specific.usage: Target: Recognize this pronunciation in Portugal speech.

common.sentence: Em Lisboa, Ana diz: «Preciso de papel.»

language_specific.pronunciation: Target: In Lisbon speech, final l in papel is velarized [ɫ] before the pause; in São Paulo it is commonly [w].
language_specific.usage: Target: Recognize the final sound in this Portugal pronunciation.

common.sentence: Em Lisboa, Marta diz: «Esse facto mudou a minha opinião.»

language_specific.pronunciation: Target: In this Portugal pronunciation, facto has a pronounced [kt] cluster; the usual São Paulo spelling fato lacks c.
language_specific.usage: Target: Recognize this Portugal form for a fact.

common.sentence: Em Faro, Luís diz: «Estou constipado e tenho o nariz entupido.»

language_specific.grammar: Target: Masculine singular adjective describing Luís.
language_specific.usage: Target: Constipado can mean having a cold in Portugal; resfriado is common in Brazil.

common.sentence: Em Lisboa, Ana diz: «A parede azul precisa de tinta.»

language_specific.pronunciation: Target: In connected Portugal speech, the final unstressed e of parede may be elided before the vowel in azul.
language_specific.usage: Target: Recognize the written word when its final vowel is absent in connected speech.

common.sentence: Em Faro, Ana diz: «A Eva deu-me mapas.»

language_specific.pronunciation: Target: in careful Portugal speech, unstressed enclitic me can be [mɨ] before the immediately following consonant [m] of mapas; weakening varies.
language_specific.grammar: Target: The indirect object pronoun follows the finite verb and refers to the speaker.
language_specific.usage: Target: Enclisis is standard in Portugal.

common.sentence: Em Lisboa, Ana diz: «O Rui pediu a chave; entreguei-lha pessoalmente.»

language_specific.pronunciation: Target: In careful Portugal speech, unstressed lha can be realized as [ʎɐ] before the consonant in pessoalmente.
language_specific.grammar: Target: Enclitic lha combines lhe, referring to Rui, with a, referring to the key.
language_specific.usage: Target: Recognize this fused clitic in Portugal speech.
